title: Writing technical proposals
description: Learn how to write proposals that get approval, align teams, and make technical decisions transparent and repeatable.

data.text: Technical proposals are not just paperwork. They are how senior engineers turn ideas into action, align stakeholders, and build a record of why decisions were made. A good proposal saves weeks of confusion. A bad proposal leads to endless meetings, second-guessing, and rework.
Writing a good proposal is simpler than it sounds. Start with the problem, explain the options you considered, describe the recommended approach, and be honest about the trade-offs.
The structure of a good proposal

items: Title and summary: one or two sentences that explain what you are proposing and why it matters.
Problem: describe the current pain point with enough detail that someone unfamiliar with the issue can understand it.
Options: list two or three realistic alternatives, including the option of doing nothing.
Recommendation: explain which option you prefer and why.
Trade-offs: be honest about the costs, risks, and limitations of the recommended option.
Plan: outline the steps, timeline, and who needs to be involved.
Success criteria: define how you will know whether the project worked.

data.text: Every technical choice has downsides. Faster development may mean more technical debt. Better performance may mean higher infrastructure cost. Hiding the downsides destroys trust. When you name them yourself, you show that you have thought through the decision carefully.

data.title: Trade-off table example
data.code:
Option A: Build in-house
- Pros: Full control, no vendor dependency
- Cons: Six months of engineering time, ongoing maintenance

Option B: Use a managed service
- Pros: Ship in two weeks, vendor handles maintenance
- Cons: Monthly cost, vendor lock-in risk

data.text: Busy stakeholders will not read a ten-page document. Use headings, bullet points, tables, and bold text to make the key points easy to find. Put the summary at the top so someone with two minutes can still make an informed decision.

data.title: One-page test
data.text: Try to fit the core of your proposal on one page: problem, option, recommendation, trade-off, and next step. If you cannot, the proposal may still be too vague or too broad.

data.title: Key takeaways
data.text: A good proposal aligns the team around a shared problem and a clear path forward. Define the problem, compare real options, name the trade-offs honestly, and keep it scannable. Your goal is to make the right decision easy to approve.
